Flow cytometry. It's an analytical method that counts and sorts individual cells or particles based on their size, granularity, and fluorescence. Cells are stained with fluorescent-labeled antibodies, drawn in a single-file stream through a laser beam, and detected in real time, enabling rapid profiling of cell populations and isolation of specific subsets. Cells are suspended in fluid and forced through a narrow channel called sheath fluid so they pass one at a time through a laser. Forward scatter, which is light bending straight ahead, correlates with cell size, while side scatter—light diffracted at ninety degrees—reflects internal complexity including granularity and DNA content. Cells are stained with fluorescent antibodies, like anti-CD4 for T cells, and each antibody-dye combination excites at a different wavelength, allowing simultaneous detection of multiple markers through multicolor panels. As each cell passes through the laser, emitted light is collected by detectors and converted to digital signals, with tens of thousands of cells analyzed per second. Selected populations, such as CD4-positive T cells, can be electronically sorted into separate collection tubes for downstream culture or analysis. Flow cytometry is used in immunology for T-cell counts in HIV patients, in cancer diagnostics for leukemia classification, in vaccine development, and in basic cell biology. This technique connects to cells as the unit of analysis where each event in the cytometer represents one cell, fluorescence as the detection principle where fluorescent dyes emit light when excited, antibodies as staining reagents that bind cell-surface or intracellular antigens, and immunology as the underlying principle often used to profile immune cell populations and their activation states.
